entries.title: The watch and the town's defences
q: how do i defend my village
how do i keep monsters out
entries.answer: A town defends itself: guards walk the watch, and from the Stone Age it has a wall, gates and an alarm bell. You don't need to do anything.
more: A town sees to its own safety.

Guards (twice a folk's health) walk the watch; streets are lit with torches, then lamp posts; from the Stone Age a wall with gates shut at dusk, watch posts and an alarm bell; an Iron Age town keeps an iron golem.
When trouble comes the bell rings, gates shut, guards man the walls and everyone else goes indoors.
tips: The elder orders 'Man the walls' after lives were lost or the bell rang.
Kill monsters near folk yourself and the town thanks you.

entries.title: The night watch: rounds, lanterns and the bell
q: what do guards do at night
why did the bell ring at night
entries.answer: Once the town wall is begun, the guards on wall duty keep the night: rounds on the wall walk and posts at the gates, lanterns in hand, a bell when trouble is seen, the watch handed over at dusk, midnight and dawn.
more: The night's posts go round the wall: each side's wall walk and each gate. The guards the roster has on the walls take them in order; the first watch keeps them from dusk to midnight, the second from midnight to dawn.

A guard on a wall walk climbs the steps by its gate and walks its side end to end and back, stopping to look out over the battlements. If it cannot get up, it walks the street inside that side instead. A gate guard stands inside the gate and challenges anyone after dark.
Every guard on watch carries a lantern from the stores (a torch if there is none), so you can follow them on the wall at night.

A watchman who sees raiders, or six monsters or more, rings the town's bell: the gates shut and the town musters. One who sees a monster or two calls it and rings its handbell, and the watch goes after it.

At dusk the captain calls the first watch to its posts; as each post changes hands the two guards pass a word; at midnight the second watch takes over; at dawn the watch stands down and the gates open. All of it goes in the night's log.
steps: Open the village board: Town → Defences.
The rota lists each post, who keeps it on each watch and who is on it now (with a lantern).
Show me on a post marks its round; the night's log is below.
tips: Midnight on the wall: the watchmen call 'Midnight, and all's well!'

entries.title: Raids and the alarm bell
entries.answer: About one night in five a walled town is raided. The bell rings, gates shut and guards man the walls; help and the town thanks you.
more: About one night in five a walled town of ten or more with a watch is raided: a band (zombies and a skeleton in the Stone Age, spiders joining in the Iron Age, pillagers and vindicators from the Diamond Age) comes at a gate after dark.
The bell rings when four or more monsters get inside the wall or raiders are sighted; guards with bows shoot from the posts.
tips: Kill raiders and every folk thinks better of you; a raid night doubles the bounty.
There are no raids on Peaceful; an operator can turn them off in the config.

entries.title: Crime, the watch's cases and special constables
q: how do i arrest a folk
entries.answer: Now and then a folk steals or vandalises, and the watch investigates and takes it to court. Ask a guard 'Report a crime' or 'Swear me in'.
more: Now and then a poor or bitter folk pickpockets, steals, vandalises or forges coin.
The watch (the constable from the Iron Age) investigates clues and witnesses, names a culprit, and the council holds court.
A citizen or friend with a clean record can ask a guard 'Swear me in' to get a Constable's Badge.
steps: Talk → Town → The watch → Seen anything? / Report a crime.
To become a special constable: Town → The watch → Swear me in.
With the badge: right-click a culprit to arrest it; use the badge in the air to join or leave the beat.
controls: [Right-click] a folk with the Constable's Badge → arrest
tips: Footprints of mud lead from a scene until rain washes them out; a dropped keepsake names its owner.
A convicted folk may sit in the stocks on the square.

entries.title: The law, the jail and the court
q: what if i kill a villager
i hurt a villager by accident
how do i say sorry to a villager
how long is a jail sentence
can i break out of jail
how do i get a lawyer
what happens if i kill a witness
entries.answer: A crime is only known through a witness or a clue; then the watch walks you to jail in irons and the court tries you. Sentences last minutes of real play.
more: Nobody knows what you did unless a folk saw it or the watch finds a clue (boot prints by a body, who the dead was last seen with, stolen goods found on you). A witness goes to the watch when its nature lets it: honest folk soon, shy ones late, and it may tell a neighbour first.

What a witness saw dies with it if it hasn't told anyone. What it told a neighbour lives on as hearsay, worth half. Killing a witness is a murder case of its own: done cleanly it may never be solved; done sloppily it leads to an arrest for both.

Hurt a folk by accident? Talk to them and choose 'I'm sorry I hurt you' within the time shown; offering to pay the healer helps. Left alone it's a complaint, and two complaints are an assault charge. A killing always goes to court, which can find it an accident, manslaughter or murder.

Lesser charges bring a summons with a date on your planner; graver ones a warrant. A guard walks to you and puts you in irons: you're slowed and can't fight or use items, and you're led on a lead to the jail. Pulling free is resisting arrest; outrunning the watch puts your name on the board as wanted.

In jail your belongings are kept at the desk and handed back when you leave. Meals are brought; friends may pass things through the bars at visiting hours. Time counts while you're online (slower while away, as the server sets it). Breaking out is a crime.

At court: the charges, the watch's case, the witnesses one by one, the evidence, your defence (your own account, a lawyer for 15 coins, or the public defender), the jury (players on the jury roll too), the verdict and the judge's sentence: a fine, compensation, community work with the watch's broom, the stocks, days in the cells, or banishment.
Your record stays with you: it costs respect, some employers turn you away, and lenders think twice.
controls: U → Your life in town → You and the law
Town Hall → Respect → Your record and the law
Talk to any folk → Law → What's on my record?
tips: Plead guilty for a quarter off the sentence.
Giving yourself up to a guard counts in your favour.
Admins set harshness, jail length, the offline rate and whether killing players counts in mc_assistant-justice-server.toml.

entries.title: Outlaws, bounties and prisoners of war
q: i am an outlaw what do i do
entries.answer: Serious wrongdoers are outlawed and a bounty is put on them. Ask a guard 'Outlaws wanted' (Town, then The watch).
more: After a war towns hold prisoners (ask a guard 'Prisoners of war', buy a release, or get one out).
Someone who does enough wrong is outlawed: a WANTED poster goes up and its guards take them on sight.
Bring an outlaw in and claim the bounty from a guard.
As an outlaw yourself, 'Give yourself up', or ask the elder for a pardon.
controls: [Right-click] a guard → Town → The watch → Outlaws wanted · Claim a bounty · A wanted poster
Town → The watch → Give yourself up · Ask for a pardon
tips: A guard writes you a Wanted Poster; or craft a blank one (paper, an ink sac and red dye) and use it in a town.

entries.title: War between towns
q: how do i end a war
entries.answer: Towns sometimes go to war over a real grievance. Follow it on the town's books (Civic, then War), and join your town's army when it musters.
more: Wars are rare and never for nothing: two feuding neighbours, a real grievance, a hawkish elder who likes the odds, and a council that votes aye.
A herald brings an ultimatum; refused, both towns ring their bells and hang war banners.
Armies muster, march and fight battles you can watch from the hill, and a war ends at the table with a treaty.
steps: Join your town's army when it musters (you're told in chat with a horn).
Or work for peace: carry peace terms, or ask folk to make peace.
controls: Town's books → Civic → War · War map
tips: War-weariness grows every day of a war: length, cost, a short larder, lost trade.
An operator can turn wars off; then a feud stays a feud.

entries.title: The war room's map table
q: what does the map table do
see a map of the region
where are the other towns on a map
how do i see armies on the map
entries.answer: A map table shows a live map of the region: towns, borders, roads and armies. Right-click it.
more: Right-click a map table for the war room: a live map of the region as the town knows it, with towns' lands and borders, roads and trade routes, armies on the march, camps, battles, sieges, caravans, envoys, scouts, ruins, harbours and wonders.
Drag to pan, scroll (or + and −) to zoom, click a town for its card.
controls: Drag pan · [Scroll] or [+][−] zoom · click a town
tips: Craft it from 2 paper, a compass, 2 planks, a cartography table and 2 sticks.
Unknown land is left the colour of the paper.

entries.title: Neighbours, feuds and making peace
q: how do i make peace between towns
entries.answer: Neighbouring towns can be allies, friendly, wary, feuding or at war. Ask any folk 'Neighbours' (World tab).
more: Say 'make peace with Kingsgate' to urge peace in a feud, or (if you must) stir up trouble.
Envoys travel between towns with offers of trade, alliances and the business of war.

entries.title: Weapons and armour: steel, pikes, halberds, bows
q: what weapons does the mod add
entries.answer: The mod adds steel (iron and coal) with steel armour and sword, plus the pike, halberd, war hammer, longbow and arbalest.
more: Steel (an iron ingot and any coal, or blast an iron ingot) sits between iron and diamond: steel sword, helmet, chestplate, leggings and boots.

Military research adds the pike (more reach, hard on riders), halberd (reach and a steel edge), war hammer (slow but through armour), longbow (faster, harder arrows) and arbalest (a steel-strung crossbow).
tips: Recipes: pike (iron ingot, 2 sticks), halberd (2 steel, 2 sticks), war hammer (3 iron, 2 sticks), longbow (4 sticks, 3 string), arbalest (2 iron, a steel ingot, a crossbow); steel armour like iron armour in steel.
Towns muster pikes and halberds into the line and win the archers' duel with longbows and arbalests.

entries.title: A town on a war footing, scouts and spies
q: how do towns know each other's strength
entries.answer: At war a town goes on a war footing: drills, rations, bandages and arrows. Its scouts spy on the enemy.
more: At war a town stands on a war footing: the militia drills, the larder is kept for a siege, bandages and arrows are made, and the war stores fill (Wanted orders).
Scouts go out to read the enemy's strength; their reports age, and a quest may ask you to scout a rival and bring back a spy's report.

entries.title: Vassal towns, tribute and ruins
q: what happens to the losing town
entries.answer: A beaten town may become a vassal that pays tribute. The War page keeps the record.
more: A war ends at the table: terms are agreed (a border, tribute, a trade deal, satisfaction), and a beaten town may become a vassal paying tribute.
After a war come prisoners, ruins where things burned, and outlaws; the War page keeps the record.
